claims.text: Chemical dealloying of a multiphase noble-metal-based HEA precursor containing noble and sacrificial elements can produce a three-dimensional nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework is suitable for catalytic applications.
The precursor is a multiphase HEA in which noble metals such as Au, Pt, and Pd are intermixed with less-noble sacrificial elements.
A selective chemical etchant preferentially dissolves the sacrificial elements.
The noble-metal components remain intact during selective etching.
Controlled etchant concentration, treatment time, and temperature can permit selective removal without disrupting the residual structure.
Selective removal of sacrificial elements forms an interconnected three-dimensional network of ligaments and pores.
The ligaments of the resulting network are composed of the remaining noble-metal atoms.
Dissolution of less-noble elements triggers in situ reorganization of the remaining noble metals into a porous nanoframework.
The dealloyed nanoframework retains atomic-level compositional complexity.
The porous nanoframework has a high surface area.
The treated material will exhibit a three-dimensional nanoframework morphology with tunable pore and ligament sizes.
Dealloying will increase catalytic surface area relative to the as-cast precursor.
Dealloying will improve catalytic performance relative to the as-cast precursor.
Nanoframework formation requires the sacrificial elements to be sufficiently more etchable than the noble components.
The desired nanoframework will not form when composition or etching conditions do not permit selective removal.
Overly aggressive dealloying conditions may cause coarsening or collapse of the network.
